To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dry bean consumption reduces the risk factors associated with CVD and weight gain in animal models of diet-induced obesity.

short-term (7 d) feeding of a diet containing dry bean (Phaseo lus vulgaris L) reduced plasma cholesterol in both obese and non-obese rats and mice, and reduced plasma cholesterol and weight in diet-induced obese mice.
short-term feeding of dry bean reduces cholesterol levels and weight in rats and mice and these effects are mediated by mechanisms associated with cholesterol metabolism and excretion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of dry bean varieties that have the greatest potential to reduce the burden of CVD in the world.
the development of new approaches to identify the most beneficial dry beans for human health and to identify the bioactives that are responsible for the cardioprotection.
the identification and characterisation of the mechanisms by which dry beans and other legumes modulate CVD risk factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dry bean is a cardioprotective food, which may have the potential to reduce the risk of CVD and obesity.
dry bean has a beneficial effect on plasma lipids that is associated with the modulation of cholesterol metabolism.
the cardioprotectant activity of dry bean is mediated by a complex of bioactive components that include fibre, protein, phytochemicals and other components.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dry bean has the potential to be used as a functional food for the prevention of obesity and CVD.
beans are an important food that should be consumed regularly as a component of a healthy diet.
dry bean is an effective cardioprotective food, and the mechanisms of this protection include modulation of hepatic lipid biosynthesis and excretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dry bean is an excellent source of cardioprotective phytochemicals that can be used in the development of new functional foods to prevent and treat CVD and diet-induced obesity.

the cardioprotectiveness of dry beans and the weight loss experienced by obese mice fed a bean-containing diet are mediated by mechanisms other than those that account for their hypoglycaemic activity.
dry bean consumption has the potential to be used in the prevention of obesity-related CVD.
